title: Decolonisation and the Cold War

cards.h: The two big stories of the late 20th century
cards.b: Between 1945 and 1991 the colonies became states and the world split into two blocs. India was in the middle: it freed first, then led non-alignment.

War exhaustion of Britain, France and the Netherlands; rise of the USA and USSR (both anti-colonial in speech); nationalist movements; the UN Charter’s self-determination; and the example of India (1947). Methods: negotiation (India, Ghana 1957), war (Algeria 1954 to 62, Vietnam), settler resistance (Kenya, Mau Mau), settler states (Rhodesia, South Africa). Portugal clung on until 1974 (Carnation Revolution).

• 1945 to 1950s: India, Pakistan, Burma, Ceylon (1947 to 48), Indonesia (1949), Vietnam (Dien Bien Phu 1954).
  • 1960, the “Year of Africa”: 17 states.
  • 1960s to 70s: Algeria 1962, Kenya 1963, Angola and Mozambique 1975, Zimbabwe 1980, Namibia 1990.
  • South Africa’s end of apartheid (1994, Mandela).
Bandung Conference (1955), Non-Aligned Movement (Belgrade, 1961; Nehru, Tito, Nasser, Nkrumah, Sukarno).

Ideological gap between capitalism and communism; the Soviet hold on Eastern Europe; mutual fear. Churchill’s “iron curtain” speech (1946). Truman Doctrine (1947, aid to Greece and Turkey); Marshall Plan (1948, about $13 billion); Cominform; Berlin Blockade (1948 to 49) and the airlift. NATO (1949); Warsaw Pact (1955). Containment (George Kennan’s Long Telegram, 1946).

• 1949: Soviet bomb; Chinese revolution. 1950 to 53: Korean War.
  • 1956: Hungary, Suez. 1961: Berlin Wall.
  • 1962: Cuban Missile Crisis; hotline in 1963; Partial Test Ban Treaty 1963.
  • 1965 to 75: Vietnam war.
  • Détente (1970s): SALT I (1972), Helsinki Accords (1975).
  • 1979: Soviet invasion of Afghanistan; “new Cold War”.

Gorbachev (from 1985): glasnost and perestroika; INF Treaty (1987); fall of the Berlin Wall (9 November 1989); German unification (October 1990); Warsaw Pact ended (1991); failed coup (August 1991); the USSR dissolved on 26 December 1991. Reasons: economic stagnation, arms race costs, Afghanistan, nationalism, and Reagan’s pressure.

Orthodox (traditionalist) writers blamed Stalin; revisionists such as William Appleman Williams and Gabriel Kolko blamed US economic expansion; post-revisionists such as John Lewis Gaddis (We Now Know, 1997) found fault on both sides. Francis Fukuyama’s “end of history” (1989) was challenged by Huntington’s Clash of Civilizations (1993).

India’s non-alignment was a form of strategic autonomy; its 1971 treaty with the USSR; its role in Korea (Custodian Force, Chair of the Neutral Nations Repatriation Commission, K. P. S. Thimayya). Today’s “multi-alignment” and the new great-power rivalry between the US and China are debated as a possible “new Cold War”.
